subject: Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set

messages.author: 510c4faa44d51842
messages.subject: Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to estimate the genetic map for a data set of haploid
individuals. After about 24 hours of computation with the read.cross
command (no genetic or physical distances are included in the input
file) I get this message:

--Read the following data:
172 individuals
52466 markers
13 phenotypes
--Estimating genetic map
--Cross type: bc
Warning messages:
1: Didn't converge!
2: Didn't converge!
3: In summary.cross(cross) :
Some chromosomes > 1000 cM in length; there may be a problem
with the genetic map.
(Perhaps it is in basepairs?)

I don't know the large number of markers that I have makes the
computation problematic? Maybe one can tweak the parameters of the map
estimation?

On the other hand, I'm thinking that since my marker set is so dense
(one marker every ~250 bp on average) and I have very little missing
data maybe I'm as good off with simple marker regression (for which I
assume a genetic map is not used). I'm not fully read up on the more
sophisticated methods implemented in rQTL, but my feeling is that a
lot of the juice in those methods goes into more accurately locating
QTLs when you have sparse markers and potentially a lot of missing
genotype data?

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map estimation does not converge for dense marker set
parts:
If you don't provide marker positions but just chromosome IDs, read.cross will attempt to infer inter-marker distances, which can take a very long time.

I would use read.cross with estimate.map=FALSE. The markers will be assigned arbitrary genetic map locations, but you'll be able to work on estimating the map afterwards.

If you have physical positions for the markers, it's best to include them in the file, but on a Mbp scale rather than bp scale, and even better would be to use what knowledge you have of recombination rate to assign estimated genetic map positions to markers.

karl
